title: Shift Left Is Becoming A System-Level Problem
gist: A Semiconductor Engineering roundtable (Synopsys, Hiveware, Silvaco, Axiomise) argues shift left is expanding from verification to system-level validation across software, multi-physics and packaging, but fragmented tools and contexts let bugs escape. Agentic AI may coordinate disciplines and optimize tool use, yet cannot replace simulation and emulation engines.

themes.theme: Shift left expands to system validation

insights.claim: Shift left in chip design is moving beyond verification to system-level validation, and getting those decisions wrong could bankrupt small companies, according to Axiomise CEO Ashish Darbari.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: System-validation tooling becomes a high-stakes spend category for chip startups.
insights.quote: it’s influencing huge decisions that could make small companies go bankrupt if they get it wrong
insights.locator: SE: The focus of shift left in design

insights.claim: Bug escapes arise from misalignment among architects, designers and software teams even when individual components are verified, and Darbari argues this cannot be solved without bringing software into the development cycle.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Hardware-software co-validation is a key unmet need.
insights.locator: Darbari: Yes, and it’s influencing huge decisions

insights.claim: Synopsys' Frank Schirrmeister says shift left must also integrate multi-physics, including EM, thermal and mechanical, with packaging constraints that may not be solvable until a later project.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Multi-physics and packaging co-design drive demand for integrated EDA platforms.
insights.quote: It’s not only software. It’s all the other aspects, like multi-physics.

insights.claim: Silvaco's Jack Berg notes verification has traditionally been the longest and most expensive part of a design, and while chunks are shifting left, the industry lacks a single integrated workflow spanning safety, security, power, packaging and thermals.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Integration gap is an opportunity for EDA consolidation or platform plays.
insights.quote: And it really is a workflow, not just a single tool.
insights.locator: Berg: We have different aspects of that

insights.claim: Darbari recounts a design that was exhaustively formally proved yet missed a bug because the software team drove the SoC differently, losing transactions and requiring a late patch.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Formal proof of components does not guarantee system correctness.
insights.locator: I was coding for one project

insights.claim: Schirrmeister recounts an emulation case where hardware and software teams blamed the emulator vendor until they found the code region was clock-gated and powered down in the system context.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: System context (power states) must be shared across teams and with agentic AI.

themes.theme: Limits of agentic AI in EDA

insights.claim: Schirrmeister believes the underlying EDA stack of characterization, simulation and emulation will still be required; AI agents can use these engines more smartly but cannot bypass them, and engine speed has limits.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Core simulation/emulation engines (and incumbents' hardware) retain value in the AI era.
insights.quote: You can make the tool flow more productive, but the underlying engines still need to execute, and there are limits to how fast they can become.
insights.locator: Schirrmeister: There are two views here

insights.claim: Darbari warns that unless AI agents are stitched into a single context spanning manufacturing, physics, thermal, functional and software, bugs will keep creeping through the seams, raising the question of whether there is a master agent.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Multi-agent orchestration with unified context is the key missing layer in AI EDA.
insights.quote: Unless we stitch the agents in ways so that we can handle all of these challenges, there will still be bugs creeping through the seams.
insights.locator: Darbari: Unless we stitch the agents

insights.claim: Darbari argues unified cross-domain chip context is exactly what AI should be used for because it is humanly infeasible to know and derive all that information.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Positions AI as integration layer rather than replacement for engines.
insights.quote: it’s humanly not feasible to know and derive all of this information
insights.locator: Darbari: Unless we stitch the agents

insights.claim: Hiveware's Ronen Laviv suggests AI could act as a common database across verification, emulation and physical data, potentially even across companies, and could use hooks into formal and simulation tools to avoid waiting two days for tests to finish.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Tool APIs/hooks for AI agents may become a competitive EDA feature.
insights.locator: Laviv: Nowadays, with AI knowing everything

insights.claim: Historical packaging and thermal data could be used to build predictive models of what went wrong last time, but no tool yet ties functional safety, security, power, packaging and thermals into one frame.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Data reuse across projects is an untapped AI opportunity in chip design.
insights.locator: Darbari: If we pick up historical data

insights.claim: Schirrmeister says engineers can be smarter about allocating work among emulation, simulation and FPGA-based prototyping, and customers review why bugs found in simulation were not caught earlier in formal.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Engine-allocation optimization is a near-term AI use case.
insights.locator: Schirrmeister: There are certain things you can shift left

insights.claim: Laviv says chips with 200 billion transistors, citing Intel's Broadwell, strain tools that cannot run such designs without emulation, requiring the simulation environment to pull emulation in earlier.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Growing design scale sustains emulation hardware demand.
insights.quote: With chips like [Intel’s] Broadwell, with 200 billion transistors, we’ll need much more verification.

insights.claim: Axiomise's PPA analysis found unused die area burning power that synthesis does not remove and that lint and coverage do not flag, so redundant logic should be treated as an architect's or designer's problem rather than a synthesis problem.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Early architecture-level PPA analysis can recover wasted power and area.
insights.quote: Synthesis isn’t removing it. Lint isn’t telling you it’s bad. Coverage is not telling you it’s bad.
insights.locator: Darbari: We’ve been looking at the power/performance/area

insights.claim: Darbari argues that bringing what used to be verification or layout problems into the design and architecture phase is what needs to happen.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Value in EDA shifts upstream toward architecture-level tools.
insights.quote: But bringing what used to be a verification or layout problem in as a design or architecture problem is what needs to happen.
insights.locator: Darbari: We’ve been looking at the power/performance/area
